item.title: Why Split Tunneling in Android Clients Leaks
item.description:
Whitelists and autostart checkboxes in Android VPN clients create a false sense of security. Force-stop the client, and the next request silently goes through your home IP. This is a minor issue for YouTube but can lead to a permanent ban without a refund for a $200 Claude Max subscription. The problem isn't flawed client implementations but an Android limitation: split tunneling is incompatible with the system kill-switch. This article demonstrates where traffic leaks, why the DNS + SNI proxy combination fails on smartphones, and how to achieve complete isolation for neural networks. Read on.

item.title: Prompt is not a string, but a template
item.description:
The project repository contains 203 kilobytes of prompts, which is about a third of the total PHP code. However, there are no prompts directly in the code; they are all YAML files that undergo review, versioning, and release. This article breaks down the structure of such a file and explains why the unit of storage is not just text, but the entire capability: provider, model, generation parameters, and templates for each language. It also covers non-obvious aspects: why user data is substituted after template rendering rather than within it, why models need aliases, how to degrade through three levels of JSON schema support, and what can actually be tested in a non-deterministic environment. Read on.

item.title: Gartner's Hype Cycle is a Hegelian Triad. What Should an Engineer Do in the Trough of Disillusionment?
item.description:
Continuing the series on the philosophy of technology. The initial article, the most interesting in my opinion: "Blinding Algorithms, or a Monkey with a Grenade: Why We Need a Pressure Gauge, Not a Ban on AI." The second is about the decoupling of body, place, and action. The third is about another rupture: between what you want to see and what you are shown. This one—the fourth—is about the framework that encompasses all three. In any dispute about AI chat, two positions currently converge. The first: 'Agents will replace juniors in a year, it's just a matter of integration.' The second: 'It's a bubble, LLMs are a dead end, give me back deterministic code and common sense.' The arguments are usually fierce because each side is convinced they are arguing about facts. It's not about facts. It's about how any encounter between humans and new technology is structured, and it's about two hundred years old. Both positions were formulated long before electricity, both have real foundations, and both are one-sided. And the curve that consulting uses to describe hype is not a marketing metaphor. It's a Hegelian triad, redrawn on the axes of 'expectations / time.' Next, I will show where this curve comes from, why the trough of disillusionment is structurally inevitable (and not due to investor stupidity), and what 'synthesis' specifically means in engineering practice. Spoiler: it's not a 'balanced position.' 1. Two truths that don't want to know about each other Thesis: technology liberates. The lineage is venerable. Thorstein Veblen, in the early 20th century, contrasted 'industry' and 'business': engineers produce, owners extract. His project was straightforward to the point of naivety—an 'engineers' strike,' paralyzing the old order and establishing a 'council of technical specialists' to bring efficiency and abolish the idle class. The utopia didn't materialize, but a moderate version did: Daniel Bell and Alvin Toffler's post-industrial theory described a society where management separates from ownership, and human capital displaces others. And this position has a truth that technophobes systematically ignore. Lewis Mumford showed that during the transition from primitive times to ancient Eastern kingdoms, there were almost no breakthroughs in tools. The breakthrough was in the organization of activity—and it gave us cities, irrigation, and pyramids. Technology emancipates before technique does: the megamachine was assembled from people, not iron. A second, less obvious example. Marx, describing the horrors of machine production, notes that the machine made muscular strength redundant, paving the way for cheaper female and child labor. He sees only exploitation here. But the same fact has another side that he missed: women gained the ability to earn their own living. This isn't 'reducing unemployment'; it's an economic prerequisite for equality that was impossible in a patriarchal agrarian family. The same process that is experienced as a catastrophe by one segment of society opens an escape from centuries of dependence for another. Read more

item.title: How I Stopped Paying for Tokens and Built a Local RAG on 72,000 Chunks in SQLite
item.description:
I'm a 22-year-old AI/ML engineer and researcher. My projects grew, and context started to crumble. The standard advice is to use LangChain with OpenAI API and Pinecone, but I don't have money for API calls, and I didn't want to drag heavy frameworks for simple file search. So, I decided to build a fully local solution: no paid keys, no cloud vector DBs, just CPU and SQLite. Here's a breakdown of how it works, the pitfalls I encountered, and why classic RAG is useful for something different than tutorials suggest.

item.title: How I Stopped Being a Dispatcher for My AI Agents
item.description:
I used to constantly check on my AI agents, like a nervous tic. With one agent, it was simple: give a task, discuss, review code. But with multiple parallel sessions, I found myself acting as a dispatcher, moving context between planning and implementation, explaining things to reviewers. Agents took over the coding but turned me into a manager: responding to this one, watching that one, waiting for another. If left unsupervised, they could get stuck in loops or endless review cycles. I realized I was recreating the same inefficient handoffs I'd tried to eliminate in human development. The key is to separate roles only where it's beneficial and ensure context flows smoothly without my constant intervention. For example, separating verification from implementation is useful when errors are costly, like in the evaluator-optimizer pattern where one AI checks another's work. A large context window doesn't solve the problem of AI losing details or getting stuck; separate reviewers with clear criteria and diffs work better. I explored various agent orchestration tools, finding many to be rushed and unreliable. I settled on Multica for development, OpenBot for personal tasks, and Paseo as a backup. The main benefit has been reclaiming my time and attention, no longer needing to constantly monitor the agents. The focus should be on how much time and attention we gain back, not just how many agents are running.

item.title: [Translation] Fine-tuning a Small Language Model on a Mac for RAG in the Browser
item.description:
The task seemed quite simple: fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B to answer questions based on text snippets found through semantic search. But initial experiments had the opposite effect: the model started to make up details more often, even though the validation loss continued to decrease. Four versions of the training data helped to understand why this was happening and how to reduce hallucinations by threefold, albeit at the cost of more frequent refusals to answer. See the results

item.title: Gemini 4 Neon has caught up to Opus 5.5, but almost no one noticed the release
item.description:
A week ago, I would have laughed in the face of anyone who said I'd be praising Google's neural network. The market had long since shrunk to Opus 5.5 at the top and endless arguments with ChatGPT at the bottom. And then Gemini 4 Neon came out: a "mid-tier" model that understands tasks with half a word, fixes bugs in others' MCP adapters itself, and finds server performance bottlenecks that have been sought for three weeks. I'll tell you why there's silence around the release, what Google just fixed in the Antigravity cache, and where Neon's weak spots lie. See tests and numbers

item.title: The Whale Swam into the World of Agents: What Actually Changed in Docker After "Run on Trust"
item.description:
Even Docker, which seemed like the eternal foundation under any project, is changing in the wake of AI. On November 19th, the company changed its whale and slogan, and the first screen of docker.com is now entirely about agents. Meanwhile, half of the products marked "New" were released back in the summer. Let's see what has actually changed, what you can install for free, and where the whale is swimming. Read more
